project_metadata.title: C Compiler in Rust
project_metadata.topic: Building a production-ready C compiler written in Rust
project_metadata.goal: Ship an open-source C compiler in Rust that is educational, well-tested, and production-grade — targeting x86_64 with a clean architecture that enables multi-backend support

decisions.label: Decision: C11 target standard
decisions.content: Decision: Target C11 as the initial standard. This includes _Generic, _Static_assert, _Atomic, anonymous structs/unions, alignas/alignof. The architecture must support the full C11 feature set. This matches rcc's target and provides a complete, practical compiler.

decisions.label: Decision: Multi-backend (x86-64, ARM64, RISC-V)
decisions.content: Decision: Multi-backend from the start. x86-64, ARM64 (AArch64), and RISC-V backends. Emit assembly text and use external assembler/linker (as + ld). Define a clean Backend trait/interface so codegen is abstracted. Each backend implements: register allocation, instruction selection, calling convention, assembly emission. This matches rcc's approach but with assembly emission instead of direct machine code.

decisions.label: Decision: Integrated C preprocessor
decisions.content: Decision: Integrated C preprocessor. Full preprocessor including #include, #define (function-like + object-like), conditional compilation (#ifdef/#ifndef/#endif/#elif/#else), #pragma, token pasting (##), stringizing (#), variadic macros (__VA_ARGS__), and #error/#warning. The preprocessor is a separate phase that produces a token stream for the parser. This makes the compiler self-contained — no external cpp needed.

decisions.label: Decision: SSA-based IR architecture
decisions.content: Decision: SSA-based IR. The compiler pipeline: Source -> Preprocessor -> Lexer -> Parser -> Semantic Analysis -> AST -> SSA IR -> Optimizations -> Backend (x86-64/ARM64/RISC-V). SSA provides clean separation between frontend and backend. Each backend implements a trait that consumes SSA, not AST. This enables: (1) meaningful optimizations on SSA, (2) multi-backend support without duplicating frontend logic, (3) educational value — SSA is the standard IR in modern compilers.

decisions.label: Decision: 11 standard optimization passes
decisions.content: Decision: Standard optimizations at launch — 11 optimization passes on the SSA IR: (1) constant folding, (2) constant propagation, (3) dead code elimination, (4) common subexpression elimination, (5) loop-invariant code motion, (6) strength reduction, (7) register allocation (linear scan), (8) peephole optimization, (9) function inlining (simple), (10) tail call optimization, (11) basic block reordering. This matches rcc's optimization level and produces genuinely good code. All optimizations operate on SSA form.

decisions.label: Decision: 9-crate workspace structure
decisions.content: Decision: Cargo workspace with 9 crates: (1) rcc_common — shared types, error handling, diagnostics, source location tracking, (2) rcc_lexer — tokenizer/lexer, (3) rcc_preprocessor — full C preprocessor, (4) rcc_parser — recursive descent parser and AST definition, (5) rcc_sema — semantic analysis, type checking, symbol table, (6) rcc_ir — SSA IR definition and AST-to-SSA conversion, (7) rcc_opt — 11 optimization passes on SSA, (8) rcc_codegen — Backend trait + x86-64/ARM64/RISC-V implementations, (9) rcc_driver — CLI driver. Plus a top-level rcc crate that re-exports the library for users who want to use it as a library.

decisions.label: Decision: Comprehensive 5-layer testing
decisions.content: Decision: Comprehensive testing at launch. Five layers: (1) Unit tests in every crate following TDD, (2) Integration tests that compile C files, assemble, link, and run them checking stdout/exit code, (3) chibicc test suite (41 tests — the de facto standard for small C compilers), (4) Differential testing against GCC/Clang — compile same C file with both compilers, run both binaries, assert identical output, (5) Fuzzing with cargo-fuzz targeting lexer and parser. Differential testing is the key differentiator that catches codegen bugs unit tests miss.

decisions.label: Decision: Project name — Kestrel
decisions.content: Decision: Project name is "kestrel". Distinctive, memorable, no naming conflicts. Short, easy to type and search. The CLI binary will be `kestrel`, the GitHub repo will be `durgesh-k-sharma/kestrel`, the crate prefix will be `kestrel_` (e.g., kestrel_lexer, kestrel_parser, kestrel_codegen).

decisions.label: Decision: Dual MIT/Apache 2.0 license
decisions.content: Decision: Dual MIT/Apache 2.0 license. The Rust ecosystem standard — maximizes adoption while providing patent protection. Same license as rustc, tokio, serde. Users can choose either license.

decisions.label: Decision: GCC-compatible CLI + subcommands
decisions.content: Decision: GCC-compatible CLI with rich subcommands. GCC flags: -c (compile only), -S (emit assembly), -E (preprocess only), -O0/-O1/-O2 (optimization level), -g (debug info), -o (output), --target (x86_64/arm64/riscv64). Subcommands: compile (default — full pipeline), check (parse + semantic analysis only, no codegen), preprocess (preprocessor only), ast (dump AST), ir (dump SSA IR), asm (dump assembly). This gives users the familiar GCC interface plus educational/debugging subcommands.

decisions.label: Decision: Library + CLI
decisions.content: Decision: Both library and CLI. The 8 core crates form the reusable library. kestrel_driver is a thin CLI wrapper. This enables: (1) embedding in other Rust programs, (2) LSP server for IDE integration, (3) easier programmatic testing, (4) other tools building on top (static analyzers, formatters). Users can `use kestrel_lexer::Lexer;` etc. A top-level `kestrel` crate re-exports the full library API for convenience.

decisions.label: Decision: Full CI/CD from day one
decisions.content: Decision: Full CI/CD from day one. GitHub Actions workflows: (1) CI — cargo check, cargo test, cargo clippy, cargo fmt --check, build all targets, chibicc test suite, differential tests against GCC, (2) Release — on tag push, build release binaries for Linux (x86_64, ARM64), macOS (x86_64, ARM64), Windows (x86_64), create GitHub Release with artifacts, publish to crates.io, (3) Coverage — cargo-llvm-cov, 80%+ target, coverage badge, (4) Docs — cargo doc on every push, hosted on GitHub Pages. Pre-commit hooks via husky-style setup: cargo fmt, cargo clippy, cargo check.

decisions.label: Decision: Vertical slice milestones M0-M10
decisions.content: Decision: Vertical slice milestones M0-M10. M0: Scaffold — workspace, CI/CD, project structure, hello world. M1: Lexer + Preprocessor — tokenize and preprocess C source. M2: Parser — parse C11 grammar into AST. M3: Semantic analysis — type checking, symbol table. M4: SSA IR — AST to SSA conversion. M5: x86-64 backend — emit x86-64 assembly from SSA (first working compiler — can compile and run simple C programs). M6: Optimizations — 11 optimization passes on SSA. M7: ARM64 backend. M8: RISC-V backend. M9: Standard library / runtime — minimal libc. M10: Polish — LSP server, documentation, crates.io publish. Each milestone produces a testable, demonstrable artifact. Working compiler achieved at M5.

risks.label: Risk: C preprocessor complexity
risks.content: Risk: C preprocessor complexity. The C preprocessor is essentially a separate language with token pasting, stringizing, variadic macros, and recursive expansion rules. It's ~30-40% of total compiler complexity. Mitigation: Implement in a separate crate (kestrel_preprocessor) with extensive unit tests. Reference: the C99/C11 standard sections 6.10.x. Use the chibicc test suite for validation.

risks.label: Risk: SSA IR construction correctness
risks.content: Risk: SSA IR construction correctness. Converting AST to SSA form requires correct dominance frontier computation, phi node placement, and variable renaming. Bugs here cause silent miscompilation. Mitigation: Extensive unit tests for SSA construction, validate SSA invariants after construction, differential testing against GCC from M5 onward.

risks.label: Risk: Multi-backend calling conventions
risks.content: Risk: Multi-backend calling conventions. Each target (x86-64, ARM64, RISC-V) has different calling conventions, register sets, and ABI requirements. Getting these wrong causes subtle bugs. Mitigation: Start with x86-64 System V ABI (most documented), use differential testing, reference the official ABI specifications for each target.

risks.label: Risk: Scope creep
risks.content: Risk: Scope creep. C11 is a large standard. It's tempting to implement everything at once. Mitigation: Strict milestone boundaries. Each milestone has a clear "done" criterion. Features not in the current milestone are deferred. The M5 goal is a working compiler for a C11 subset — not full C11.

required_skills.label: Skill mapping for Kestrel
required_skills.content:
Skills required for Kestrel execution:
- Phase 0 (Research): browser_navigate, terminal, forge-memory MCP
- Phase 1 (Grilling): forge-memory MCP (init_session, record_qa, add_memory_node, add_memory_edge, generate_dossier)
- Phase 2 (Execution):
  - writing-plans: Write implementation plans for each milestone
  - subagent-driven-development: Execute tasks via delegate_task subagents
  - tdd: Test-driven development for each crate
  - check-compiler-errors: Rust type checking after code changes
  - requesting-code-review: Pre-commit verification
  - verify-this: Verify critical claims
  - thermos: Parallel security + quality review
  - deslop: Remove AI code slop
  - make-pr-easy-to-review: PR cleanup
  - new-branch-and-pr: Branch + PR creation
  - loop-on-ci: Monitor CI until green
  - review-and-ship: Final review and merge
  - github-repo-management: Create GitHub repo
  - github-label-setup: Set up triage labels
  - github-issues: Issue management
  - systematic-debugging: Root cause debugging
  - compiler-construction: Compiler-specific patterns
  - code-quality-review: Structured code review
  - setup-pre-commit: Husky pre-commit hooks
